The post NVIDIA Releases Alpamayo 2 Edge: A 2B Reasoning VLA for DRIVE Thor appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> NVIDIA has released Alpamayo 2 Edge , a compact reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) model for autonomous driving. Alpamayo 2 Edge is a 2B-parameter model that plans trajectories and explains them inside the vehicle. It targets NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor , not a datacenter GPU. The goal: reasoning-based planning within onboard compute and latency budgets. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 2B-class. Card breakdown: 2.45B backbone + 0.2B action expert (HF metadata says 3B). Context length: not disclosed (measured prompt: 3,236 tokens). Runs on: NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor with the FP8 + TensorRT Edge-LLM recipe. BF16 PyTorch needs 16 GB+ GPU memory, validated on 1x H100 80GB. Performance: Strong closed-loop driver for its size; mid-pack on reasoning QA. Best: 15.15 km per at-fault incident in AlpaSim, about 60x Qwen-Drive-1.0 4B (0.25 km). Worst: nuReasoning numeric score of 48.67; LingoQA 75.2 trails Alpamayo 2 Super (79.2). Bottom line: Best: reasoning-based planning at 160 to 190 ms on in-car hardware. Worst: only H100 validated, and real-time Thor speed needs the FP8 recipe. What is Alpamayo 2 Edge? Alpamayo 2 Edge is an open NVIDIA VLA model that turns surround-camera video into a 6.4-second plan. It is the in-car member of the Alpamayo family , next to the 34B cloud model Alpamayo 2 Super . Per the model card , the 2.45B backbone pairs a 1.96B language model with a 0.41B SigLIP2 encoder. A 0.2B diffusion action expert sits on top. The backbone comes from NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge and is Nemotron-based. NVIDIA markets the model as 2B, while Hugging Face metadata shows 3B. What goes in and what comes out? For trajectory prediction, the model reads 6 cameras and 22 frames per observation. The 2 front cameras give 5 frames each, the other 4 give 3 each. It also takes a navigation instruction and 20 historical ego poses. Output is 64 waypoints from 0.1 to 6.4 seconds. The action expert predicts acceleration and curvature, then a unicycle model integrates them. The text output is a Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning trace. The model also answers free-form questions about a driving scene. How does adaptive reasoning work? During routine driving, the model emits special <NOMINAL> tokens instead of a full reasoning trace. It writes CoC reasoning only when a scene needs it. Fewer tokens means less compute per planning step. How was Alpamayo 2 Edge trained? NVIDIA team lists these ingredients: Offline distillation from CoC autolabels generated by Alpamayo 2 Super. About 115,000 hours of multi-camera driving video and about 3.7M CoC traces. Closed-loop RL post-training in AlpaGym , learning from its own actions in simulation. Multi-resolution inputs for cheaper encoding of surround views. How fast does it run on DRIVE AGX Thor? Hugging Face weights ship in BF16 and run as a PyTorch model. Real-time use on Thor needs the Alpamayo Developer Hub recipe. It stages the checkpoint and the DFlash2 drafter, then calibrates FP8 scales. Next it exports ONNX graphs and builds TensorRT engines with TensorRT Edge-LLM plugins. NVIDIA reports 160 ms to 190 ms pixel-to-trajectory latency, depending on how much the model reasons. The reference setup is DRIVE AGX Thor-X with DRIVE OS 7.2.7.0, CUDA 13.4 and TensorRT 11.3.1.9. In NVIDIA’s demo video , PyTorch BF16 plans at 0.76 Hz. The optimized FP8 Thor pipeline plans at 13.02 Hz in AlpaSim. Partner Embedl says it reached 10 Hz on AGX Thor in under 48 hours. On a workstation GPU, the card recommends at least 16 GB of memory. NVIDIA measured 12.06 GiB peak process memory on 1 H100 with 6 trajectory candidates. Other GPU architectures are not yet validated. How does Alpamayo 2 Edge score on benchmarks? NVIDIA compares Edge with Alibaba’s 4B Qwen-Drive-1.0 . In AlpaSim closed-loop driving, Edge covers 15.15 km between at-fault incidents versus 0.25 km. That is about 60x. Open-loop minADE is 0.53 m versus 1.68 m. Both are NVIDIA’s own runs. The model card adds: AlpaSim: 15.15 ± 0.04 km per at-fault incident over 875 NuRec scenarios, 3 rollouts. Open-loop minADE_6 at 5 s: 0.52 m on 1,392 PhysicalAI-AV samples. LingoQA (Lingo-Judge): 75.2. SURDS: 86.50, KITScenes scene: 89.46, nuReasoning numeric: 48.67. newContent: MarkTechPost https://www.marktechpost.com/ An Artificial Intelligence News Platform Mon, 23 Nov 2026 08:24:59 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 https://www.marktechpost.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/cropped-Favicon-512-x-512-1-1-32x32.png MarkTechPost https://www.marktechpost.com/ 32 32 127842392 Meta TLX Brings Warp-Group GPU Control to Triton on Hopper, Blackwell, AMD https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/11/23/meta-tlx-triton-low-level-extensions/ Mon, 23 Nov 2026 08:24:57 +0000 https://www.marktechpost.com/?p=84054 Meta has detailed TLX, its Triton Low-Level Extensions that add warp-group, barrier, TMA and cluster control to Python Triton kernels. It runs Meta's ads and LLM workloads on Hopper, Blackwell and AMD MI350 GPUs. The post Meta TLX Brings Warp-Group GPU Control to Triton on Hopper, Blackwell, AMD appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta has published a detailed report on TLX (Triton Low-Level Extensions) . It is the GPU compiler extension behind Meta’s production ML kernels. Meta TLX is a Triton extension that exposes warp groups, barriers, TMA and clusters to Python kernels. It targets NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell plus AMD MI300 and MI350-series GPUs. For kernel engineers, the message is CUDA-level control without leaving Triton. TL;DR What it is: an extension to Triton, not a new language. A Blackwell GEMM takes roughly 200 lines of Python-level Triton . Runs on: NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200, GB200), AMD MI300 and MI350-series. MIT-licensed. Performance: within -0.9% to +3.7% of cuBLAS on 6 H100 FP16 GEMM shapes ( PyTorch ). Best: a 4x speedup on an H100 linear compression kernel for ads inference ( Meta ). Worst: dense LLM-style attention forward reaches about 87% of FlashAttention-4 on B200 ( PyTorch ). Bottom line: Best: hand-tuned performance from short Triton code. Worst: all numbers are self-reported, with no independent benchmarks yet. What is TLX and what problem does it solve? Triton programs GPUs at the block level. CUDA programs them at the thread level. Modern GPUs need something in between. Hopper introduced warp specialization and the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA). Blackwell added tensor memory (TMEM), cluster execution and paired-CTA execution. Meta says CUDA could express these patterns, but only with large amounts of architecture-specific code. TLX fills that gap with a model the research team calls MIMW (Multi-Instruction, Multi-Warp) . The warp group becomes the basic unit of orchestration. Triton still defines what runs. TLX defines how it is orchestrated. Engineers write ordinary Triton and add TLX calls only where control matters. How does TLX work? TLX adds 5 extension areas on top of Triton: Warp-group orchestration: warp groups get roles such as producer, consumer and epilogue. Synchronization: warp groups sync through hardware mbarriers. Thread-level sync stays with the compiler. Memory orchestration: direct access to TMA, asynchronous tensor-core ops and TMEM. Cluster execution: multiple CTAs cooperate through distributed shared memory and cluster-wide barriers. Optional layouts: the compiler infers layouts. Programmers override them only for speed. The API reads like Triton. Meta’s Blackwell matmul example uses tlx.local_alloc , tlx.alloc_barriers , tlx.async_task , tlx.async_dot and tlx.barrier_wait . How fast is TLX? Benchmarks All figures below are self-reported by Meta: H100 GEMM: across 6 FP16 shapes, TLX lands between -0.9% and +3.7% of cuBLAS. On 8192x8192x8192 it reaches 577.0 TFLOPS versus 582.3 for cuBLAS ( PyTorch ). MI350 GEMM: TLX beats rocBLAS by 11.8% to 15.2% on square shapes from 256 to 2048. B200 attention: On production jagged shapes, Meta’s Jagged Flash Attention beats FlashAttention-4 by about 13% forward. Backward runs about 50% faster. On dense LLM-style shapes, forward reaches about 87% of FA4 ( PyTorch ). Code size: that attention kernel is about 3.2K lines. Meta estimates FA4 at 10K lines of CuTe DSL. The research team adds that TLX trails state-of-the-art attention most on the smallest causal-forward cases. The gap narrows as sequence length grows. Where is TLX used in production at Meta? Meta’s engineering post lists 3 case studies: Generative Ads Model (GEM) training: 20% to 25% end-to-end MFU on thousands of GPUs. TLX delivered up to 2x forward speedup for Generalized Dot Product Attention. In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO): a warp-specialized linear compression kernel hit 4x speedup on H100. FlashAttention under IKBO cut compute-intensive net latency by up to two-thirds. Distributed grouped GEMM: fuses mixture-of-experts matmuls with communication for LLM pretraining on Blackwell. Meta gives no speedup figure. Meta also compared CUTLASS, CuTe DSL and TLX on Blackwell for GEM. It says TLX gave the best productivity-performance balance for most kernels, but shares no numbers. How do developers install and use TLX? TLX lives in Meta’s MIT-licensed Triton fork, facebookexperimental/triton , under third_party/tlx/ . It also ships as triton-utlx on PyPI, a plugin for upstream Triton. The PyTorch-Triton 3.7 plugin system loads TLX without forking Triton. AMD has also published a GEMM plus activation guide for CDNA4 with TLX . It runs Meta's ads and LLM workloads on Hopper, Blackwell and AMD MI350 GPUs. The post Meta TLX Brings Warp-Group GPU Control to Triton on Hopper, Blackwell, AMD appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta has published a detailed report on TLX (Triton Low-Level Extensions) . It is the GPU compiler extension behind Meta’s production ML kernels. Meta TLX is a Triton extension that exposes warp groups, barriers, TMA and clusters to Python kernels. It targets NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell plus AMD MI300 and MI350-series GPUs. For kernel engineers, the message is CUDA-level control without leaving Triton. TL;DR What it is: an extension to Triton, not a new language. A Blackwell GEMM takes roughly 200 lines of Python-level Triton . Runs on: NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200, GB200), AMD MI300 and MI350-series. MIT-licensed. Performance: within -0.9% to +3.7% of cuBLAS on 6 H100 FP16 GEMM shapes ( PyTorch ). Best: a 4x speedup on an H100 linear compression kernel for ads inference ( Meta ). Worst: dense LLM-style attention forward reaches about 87% of FlashAttention-4 on B200 ( PyTorch ). Bottom line: Best: hand-tuned performance from short Triton code. Worst: all numbers are self-reported, with no independent benchmarks yet. What is TLX and what problem does it solve? Triton programs GPUs at the block level. CUDA programs them at the thread level. Modern GPUs need something in between. Hopper introduced warp specialization and the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA). Blackwell added tensor memory (TMEM), cluster execution and paired-CTA execution. Meta says CUDA could express these patterns, but only with large amounts of architecture-specific code. TLX fills that gap with a model the research team calls MIMW (Multi-Instruction, Multi-Warp) . The warp group becomes the basic unit of orchestration. Triton still defines what runs. TLX defines how it is orchestrated. Engineers write ordinary Triton and add TLX calls only where control matters. How does TLX work? TLX adds 5 extension areas on top of Triton: Warp-group orchestration: warp groups get roles such as producer, consumer and epilogue. Synchronization: warp groups sync through hardware mbarriers. Thread-level sync stays with the compiler. Memory orchestration: direct access to TMA, asynchronous tensor-core ops and TMEM. Cluster execution: multiple CTAs cooperate through distributed shared memory and cluster-wide barriers. Optional layouts: the compiler infers layouts. Programmers override them only for speed. The API reads like Triton. Meta’s Blackwell matmul example uses tlx.local_alloc , tlx.alloc_barriers , tlx.async_task , tlx.async_dot and tlx.barrier_wait . How fast is TLX? Benchmarks All figures below are self-reported by Meta: H100 GEMM: across 6 FP16 shapes, TLX lands between -0.9% and +3.7% of cuBLAS. On 8192x8192x8192 it reaches 577.0 TFLOPS versus 582.3 for cuBLAS ( PyTorch ). MI350 GEMM: TLX beats rocBLAS by 11.8% to 15.2% on square shapes from 256 to 2048. B200 attention: On production jagged shapes, Meta’s Jagged Flash Attention beats FlashAttention-4 by about 13% forward. Backward runs about 50% faster. On dense LLM-style shapes, forward reaches about 87% of FA4 ( PyTorch ). Code size: that attention kernel is about 3.2K lines. Meta estimates FA4 at 10K lines of CuTe DSL. The research team adds that TLX trails state-of-the-art attention most on the smallest causal-forward cases. The gap narrows as sequence length grows. Where is TLX used in production at Meta? Meta’s engineering post lists 3 case studies: Generative Ads Model (GEM) training: 20% to 25% end-to-end MFU on thousands of GPUs. TLX delivered up to 2x forward speedup for Generalized Dot Product Attention. In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO): a warp-specialized linear compression kernel hit 4x speedup on H100. FlashAttention under IKBO cut compute-intensive net latency by up to two-thirds. Distributed grouped GEMM: fuses mixture-of-experts matmuls with communication for LLM pretraining on Blackwell. Meta gives no speedup figure. Meta also compared CUTLASS, CuTe DSL and TLX on Blackwell for GEM. It says TLX gave the best productivity-performance balance for most kernels, but shares no numbers. How do developers install and use TLX? TLX lives in Meta’s MIT-licensed Triton fork, facebookexperimental/triton , under third_party/tlx/ . It also ships as triton-utlx on PyPI, a plugin for upstream Triton. The PyTorch-Triton 3.7 plugin system loads TLX without forking Triton. AMD has also published a GEMM plus activation guide for CDNA4 with TLX . TLX vs Gluon vs CuTe DSL vs TileLang Feature Meta TLX Gluon CuTe DSL TileLang Maintainer Meta with UC San Diego ( paper ) Triton project NVIDIA tile-ai open source project Approach Extension on top of Triton; warp-group orchestration; layouts optional Lower-level Triton dialect; tensors carry explicit layouts ( AMD ) Python DSL isomorphic with CuTe C++ ( FAQ ) Tile-level DSL with layout and pipeline control Hardware Hopper, Blackwell, AMD MI300 and MI350 ( Meta ) NVIDIA Hopper+ for warp specialization ( docs ); AMD MI350/MI355 ( AMD ) NVIDIA Ampere, Hopper, Blackwell CUDA, ROCm, Metal, CPU, Ascend ( SourceForge mirror ) License MIT ( repo ) MIT (part of Triton ) NVIDIA EULA for CuTe DSL files ( license ) MIT ( mirror ) Headline published result -0.9% to +3.7% vs cuBLAS, H100 FP16 GEMM Not disclosed Used for FlashAttention-4 kernels, ~10K lines per Meta’s estimate ( PyTorch ) Not disclosed Known production use Meta ads training, ads inference, LLM pretraining Not disclosed FlashAttention-4 DeepSeek TileKernels ( repo ) Key Takeaways TLX adds warp-group, barrier, TMA and cluster control to ordinary Triton code. It lands within -0.9% to +3.7% of cuBLAS on H100 FP16 GEMM. Production wins include 4x on an H100 ads kernel and 20% to 25% MFU on GEM. Dense attention forward still trails FA4 at about 87% on B200. It is MIT-licensed and loads into upstream Triton as a plugin. Check out the paper on arXiv , the Meta engineering post and the GitHub repo . The post Z AI Releases GLM-5.4: A 750B Loop Transformer That Runs 28 Layers Twice appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Z.ai has released GLM-5.4 , its first flagship model built on a Loop Transformer architecture. The GLM-5.4 Loop Transformer runs 28 layers of the GLM-5 base model for 2 iterations. Z.ai says the model reaches intelligence comparable to 2T-3T parameter models. For developers, the pitch is ‘Generalized Coding’: code as the tool for video, games, 3D shaders and CAD. TL;DR Size: 750B-scale base. Active parameters not disclosed. Context window not officially listed (the blog discusses deployment at 1M context). Runs on: Z.ai-hosted only for now (GLM Coding Plan, ZCode, Z.ai Chat). Self-hosting hardware not disclosed until weights ship. Performance: No flagship benchmark table yet. Z.ai claims parity with 2T-3T parameter models. Best: +11.3 points on AIME25 (19.17 to 30.42) in Z.ai’s 30B looped ablation. Worst: +3.3 points on IFBench (50.20 to 53.47), the smallest gain. Z.ai also flags “marathon thinking” loops. What is GLM-5.4? GLM-5.4 is a 750B-scale Loop Transformer from Z.ai that runs shared layers twice per pass. It ships first inside Z.ai’s own products: the GLM Coding Plan , the ZCode desktop app and Z.ai Chat . Z.ai did not pre-train a looped model from scratch. It adapted the pre-trained GLM-5 base through continued training. The technical post states that looped models trained from scratch still trail unshared models at equal compute. Adapting an existing base raises the ceiling with a relatively small compute overhead. How does the Loop Transformer work? In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In GLM-5.4, a group of 28 weight-shared layers runs for 2 iterations. Z.ai made 3 changes to keep this practical at 750B scale. Gated progressive updates Overwriting hidden states across loops made activation norms blow up. GLM-5.4 adds independent per-token gates for each iteration. The first pass writes small updates and builds global context. The second pass opens the gates to refine the output. On harder tokens, the first pass writes more aggressively. Hybrid KV cache A naive design keeps a full KV cache for every loop. GLM-5.4’s second loop reuses the sparse KV selected in pass 1. It keeps its own new KV only inside a local sliding window. So the extra loop costs 1 sliding window of KV cache, not a full context cache. Z.ai says this keeps the cost increase over GLM-5.3 under control at 1M context. Sparse attention index reuse The second loop reuses the indices from the first loop’s indexer. That adds zero indexing overhead. Z.ai reports near-identical results versus recomputing indices on every pass. How does GLM-5.4 perform on benchmarks? Z.ai has not published benchmark scores for the 750B GLM-5.4 model. A Z.ai team member said scores will come later, per DataCamp . The evidence in the blog is an iso-parameter ablation on a 30B model. It shares the 750B base’s architecture. The looped version used about 10% more total training compute. Scores were measured after 200K long-context SFT with thinking mode on. Benchmark (30B ablation) Baseline + Loop Gain Avg. output length change AIME25 19.17 30.42 +11.3 -635 tokens (-2%) GPQA-Diamond 47.58 56.26 +8.7 -2,473 tokens (-11.7%) AA-LCR 40.33 47.67 +7.3 -539 tokens (-9.7%) MMLU-Pro 71.65 75.05 +3.4 -863 tokens (-14.9%) IFBench 50.20 53.47 +3.3 -763 tokens (-13.0%) Source: Z.ai GLM-5.4 blog . Self-reported, 30B model, not the 750B flagship. Two patterns stand out. The largest gains come in math, science reasoning and long context. Output length also falls on most tasks. MMLU-Pro answers got 14.9% shorter and GPQA-Diamond answers 11.7% shorter. Z.ai says part of the reasoning moves into the loop’s implicit depth. AIME25 is the exception: output length dropped only 2%. Z.ai validated the design on 1B, 4B, 30B and 750B bases. The ‘2T-3T parameter’ claim has no flagship table behind it yet. What can GLM-5.4 do beyond traditional coding? Z.ai calls this direction Generalized Coding. It credits gains in both coding and vision. The technical sections shows four demos: Video: a self-narrated music video called “Hello World”. Engineering: a 6-axis robotic arm built through CAD modeling in FreeCAD. Games: a complete game with movement, physics, maps, combat and art assets. 3D: an interactive bird-watching scene built with math geometry and custom GLSL shaders. These are vendor demos, not benchmarks. How fast is GLM-5.4 and where can developers use it? Z.ai reports up to 200 tokens/s off-peak and 70-80 tokens/s at peak load. It fused core kernels to cut intermediate memory traffic. Access today runs through the GLM Coding Plan, ZCode and Z.ai Chat. ZCode is Z.ai’s desktop agent harness for GLM-5.4. It runs on macOS, Windows and Linux (Beta). The Coding Plan lists Lite at $12.6/month, Pro at $56 and Max at $117.6. Z.ai says prices may change. How does GLM-5.4 compare with other open frontier models? Should that negative sentiment and downward pressure persist, we can expect it to spill over into private markets. For this past week, however, U.S. startups continued to secure sizable rounds, led by brain-computer interface company Science landing a fresh $400 million. Another seven American companies announced venture or growth funding of $100 million or more, and across the Atlantic, UK-based AI biotech startup Isomorphic Labs landed $5 billion, the largest financing of the week. 1. Science , $400M, neurotech : Science, a startup focused on brain-computer interface technology, and neural engineering, secured $400 million in Series D funding. The round brings total funding to date for the Alameda, California-based company to more than $900 million. 2. Model ML , $250M, AI and fintech : Model ML, an AI platform for financial and professional services, closed on $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. General Atlantic and QED Investors led the round for the three-year-old company, which is based in New York and London. 3. Galvanize Therapeutics , $130M, biotech : Redwood City, California-based Galvanize Therapeutics, a developer of pulsed electric field ablation technologies for oncology and chronic disease, picked up $130 million in Series D funding led by HealthQuest Capital . 4. General Flash , $128M, critical metals : General Flash, a developer of a new method to produce critical metals, announced that it has raised $128 million across seed and Series A rounds from a long list of investors. 5. Ramon.Space , $124M, space tech : Denver-based Ramon.Space, a developer of space computing infrastructure, pulled in $124M in Series B funding led by PSG . 6. Marrow Therapeutics , $120M, biotech : Watertown, Massachusetts-based Marrow Therapeutics, a developer of bone marrow-targeted therapies to treat severe blood disorders, announced its launch with a combined $173 million in Series A and B funding. Orbimed led its $120 million Series B round while Scion Life Sciences and venBio led the $53 million Series A. 7. Noeri , $110M, enterprise AI : Noeri, a developer of self-improving AI for enterprises and researchers, launched with $110 million in initial funding. Menlo Ventures led the round for the Palo Alto-based startup, which was founded by Stanford University computer science professors. 8. Seawolf Therapeutics , $100M, biotech : San Diego-based Seawolf Therapeutics, a biotech startup developing a novel DNA delivery platform, emerged from stealth and announced that it has raised $100 million in funding to date, with Versant Ventures , MPM BioImpact and Novartis Venture Fund as lead investors. 9. BrightAI , $97M, physical AI : BrightAI, a startup developing a sensor, drone and robotics-driven platform to bring continuous observability to infrastructure-heavy industries like power, water, and energy, secured $97 million in new funding. Smith Point Capital led the financing for the Silicon Valley-based company. 10. Vincue , $93M, vehicle intelligence platform : Kansas City-based Vincue, developer of a vehicle lifecycle intelligence platform, closed on $93 million in growth capital led by Wavecrest Growth Partners . And overseas: Isomorphic Labs , $5B, AI and biotech : London-based Isomorphic Labs, a startup that applies AI to drug discovery, secured $5 billion in Series C funding. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital led the financing for the five-year-old company, which also has offices in Massachusetts and Switzerland. Check out our previous entry here . What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car? Those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a company bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a big business. Let’s take a closer look. $73.5M to reflect sunlight from space Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down. To that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset. The company recently announced $73.5 million in new funding , bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase . Existing investors Sequoia Capital , Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures , Convective Capital , The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1 . Reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it says can be launched aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The company envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark. The idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial launches, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships. The raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally , per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:36:35 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.13 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Most Unicorns Are Worth More Than Their Last Funding-Round Valuations, Crunchbase Estimates https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/unicorn-startup-current-valuations-thinking-machines-sierra-crunchbase/ Mon, 23 Nov 2026 12:00:19 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94433 The more than 1,900 startups on the The Crunchbase Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion, based on their last reported valuations. But Crunchbase’s new Current Valuation Model , which estimates how private-company values have changed since their last funding rounds, puts that figure closer to $11 trillion. Most unicorns are estimated to have gained value, even as others have lost ground, our analysis shows. Among the biggest potential gainers are AI startups Thinking Machines Lab , whose estimated value has climbed from $12 billion to $40 billion, and Sierra , from nearly $16 billion to $31.5 billion. The majority of companies on the board are valued higher by the Current Valuations model than they were when they last raised funding. Only around 236 companies — roughly 12% of the board — are down by more than $100 million in value compared to their last reported valuations. The valuation model estimates that a select group of 24 companies have gained more than $10 billion in value since their most recent funding rounds. They include Mira Murati ’s AI research lab Thinking Machines Lab, which was last valued at $12 billion in its 2025 seed funding but has a current valuation projected at $40 billion. Similarly, Bret Taylor ’s customer oriented AI agent builder Sierra was last valued at close to $16 billion in a May 2026 funding round. It is now estimated to be valued at $31.5 billion, per the Crunchbase model. (On Monday, Bloomberg reported that Sierra is raising a new round at a roughly $30 billion valuation.) Physical Intelligence , a company building AI for robotics, was valued at $5.6 billion in its Series B. Crunchbase’s Current Valuation model estimates its valuation now at $18.5 billion. Another 53 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $5 billion to just under $10 billion higher than those achieved in their most recent funding rounds. They include Unconventional AI , which is focused on energy efficiency for AI; Lila Sciences , which is building artificial intelligence for science; AI cloud company Vultr ; AI research lab humans& ; stablecoin payment platform Tempo ; and Yann LeCun ’s Advanced Machine Intelligence , which is modeling physical world intelligence. A total of 484 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $1 billion to $5 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations. More than 1,100 companies have values that were flat or up to $1 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations. Only around 236 companies are estimated to be below their most recent valuation, by more than $100 million. Collectively, their current valuations are down by $326 billion from their most recent fundings, Crunchbase estimates. Unicorn growth The Crunchbase Unicorn Board reached its highest value in 2026 as three companies approached or exceeded $1 trillion valuations — unprecedented in the board’s history. The board peaked at $10 trillion in advance of the Anthropic IPO this past week. The company’s public-market debut removed close to $1 trillion from the board. This followed another trillion-dollar exit from the board earlier this year, when SpaceX — last valued at $1.3 trillion in a secondary financing this year — before it went public in June at a value of $1.8 trillion. All told, the unicorn board this year is currently up by $1.5 trillion from its $7.5 trillion value at the end of 2025. With its closest rival now on the public markets, OpenAI is currently the most highly valued private company at an official valuation of $1.25 trillion. The unicorn board has picked up pace this year. Around 360 companies joined the board so far this year, the second highest count in a single year after 2021 when 621 companies joined. A faster pace of new entrants and rising valuations have helped replenish the board, while current estimates suggest substantial additional value has accumulated between funding rounds. The next test is how closely these estimated values align with prices investors are willing to pay. Future funding rounds, secondary transactions, public listings and M&A will reveal how much of the board’s estimated $2 trillion uplift translates into realized value.
